url-shortener.title: URL shortener
url-shortener.pitch: A short-link service for marketing campaigns: few links created, a huge number of clicks from everywhere.

static-website.title: Marketing website
static-website.pitch: A marketing site that grows: from a few static files to a contact form, global visitors and bots.

notifications.title: Notification service
notifications.pitch: Send push, email and SMS to customers without making anyone wait, even on flash sale day.

startup-api.title: Startup API
startup-api.pitch: Grow one API from launch day to thousands of requests per second, and keep the bill under control.

document-vault.title: Company document vault
document-vault.pitch: Build an internal document sharing service: files are never public, uploads are scanned for viruses, and bots cannot scrape them.

photo-sharing.title: Photo sharing
photo-sharing.pitch: People post photos, friends view them and get notified, until the day one photo goes viral.

ecommerce.title: Online shop
ecommerce.pitch: From one server to launch day: grow a 3-tier shop that survives an AZ outage, a flash sale and a flood of orders.

ticketing.title: Concert tickets
ticketing.pitch: Tens of thousands of fans hit "Buy" the second sales open: keep the ticketing system standing.

news-feed.title: Social news feed
news-feed.pitch: A feed that is read far more than it is written: caches, read replicas and the edge keep scrolling smooth for everyone.

health-records.title: Electronic health records
health-records.pitch: Build a health records portal for a clinic chain: medical data must stay encrypted, private and safe from attacks.

video-streaming.title: Course video platform
video-streaming.pitch: An e-learning platform: smooth playback on every continent, automatic transcoding of new uploads, and service that continues through a Region failure.

saas-dr.title: SaaS that never goes down
saas-dr.pitch: A B2B app that enterprise customers pay to always be up, even when an AZ or a whole Region is lost.

iot-telemetry.title: IoT telemetry
iot-telemetry.pitch: Thousands of sensors report every second; store every reading and power the dashboards without losing data.

game-leaderboard.title: Game leaderboard
game-leaderboard.pitch: Backend for a global mobile game: hot leaderboards, players everywhere, bot attacks and a whole Region going down.

banking-portal.title: Online banking portal
banking-portal.pitch: Build a banking portal that meets strict security rules and survives outages, attacks and payday.

payment-api.title: Card payment API
payment-api.pitch: Build a serverless payment API for PCI DSS: encrypt card data, stop card-testing bots and check fraud asynchronously.

clickstream.title: Real-time clickstream
clickstream.pitch: Capture every click for a dashboard and a fraud detection model: Kinesis with several consumers, data kept in the EU, encryption, backups and a traffic peak.

edge-firewall.title: Brokerage with packet inspection
edge-firewall.pitch: Build a trading platform where regulators require third-party packet inspection, partners need static IPs and institutions trade over raw TCP.

fintech-eu.title: European e-wallet
fintech-eu.pitch: Build an e-wallet on an Aurora ledger: data stays in the EU, Lambda connects through RDS Proxy and Secrets Manager, bots are blocked and US customers are served too.

hr-portal.title: Internal HR portal
hr-portal.pitch: Build a serverless HR portal: staff sign in with Cognito, read payslips from a private bucket, survive ransomware and keep data in the EU.

legacy-crm.title: Legacy CRM migration
legacy-crm.pitch: Move an old CRM to AWS as it is, then modernise it step by step to cut the bill: serverless, pooled database connections, rotated passwords and backups.

partner-api.title: B2B partner API
partner-api.pitch: Build an API for business partners: static IPs they can allow-list, rotating credentials, report files that never cross the internet, and survival against ransomware.

realtime-game.title: Real-time game
realtime-game.pitch: Multiplayer game servers over UDP: layer 4 load balancing, anycast IPs for players worldwide, a telemetry stream for anti-cheat and a Region outage mid-tournament.

render-farm.title: Video render service
render-farm.pitch: Run a container render service with no ops team: Fargate, jobs that take tens of minutes through SQS, a VPC endpoint and Spot to cut costs.

saas-billing.title: Billing SaaS
saas-billing.pitch: Run a B2B invoicing SaaS on Aurora and keep it cheap: Auto Scaling for office hours, a VPC endpoint instead of NAT, read replicas for reports, and backups.

first-users.title: Closed beta
first-users.story: The closed beta just opened to the first testers: about 50 requests per second, mostly page views and saved data.
first-users.concept: Every request needs a server (EC2) to run code and a database (RDS) to read and write.
first-users.nudge: Drag in EC2 and RDS, then connect Users → EC2 → RDS.

scale-up.title: In the local news
scale-up.story: A newspaper mentioned your app. Traffic is up to 350 req/s.
scale-up.concept: Vertical scaling: move to a bigger instance. Quick, but it has a ceiling and is still a single point of failure.
scale-up.nudge: Select EC2 and set Size to Medium. RDS needs Medium too.

scale-out.title: Top of the App Store
scale-out.story: 1,300 req/s. Even the biggest single machine blows the budget.
scale-out.concept: Horizontal scaling: several small servers behind an Application Load Balancer are cheaper and sturdier than one big box.
scale-out.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 Medium ×3 → RDS Large.

az-outage.title: An AZ loses power
az-outage.story: Everything runs nicely in us-east-1a… until today.
az-outage.concept: High availability: spread servers across 2+ AZs and turn on RDS Multi-AZ for automatic failover.
az-outage.nudge: EC2 ×2 with AZ "a+b" behind the ALB; turn on Multi-AZ for RDS.

flash-sale.title: Noon flash sale
flash-sale.story: Normally 220 req/s, but the flash sale triples it. Paying for the peak all day loses money.
flash-sale.concept: Auto Scaling Group: add instances when load rises, remove them when it falls. Pay only for what runs.
flash-sale.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling for EC2 Medium (min 1, max 3). RDS Large handles the peak.

region-down.title: The whole Region goes down
region-down.story: Your boss asks: "What if all of us-east-1 goes down?" Today you find out.
region-down.concept: Disaster recovery: run a copy in another Region (warm standby) and let Route 53 fail over when health checks fail. The database must be multi-Region out of the box: Aurora Global Database keeps a copy in the other Region and fails over in ~1 minute, with no manual promotion as with a cross-Region RDS replica.
region-down.nudge: Users → Route 53 → two ALB → EC2 stacks; put the second stack in eu-west-1. Use one Aurora, turn on Aurora Global Database, and link the EC2 in both Regions to it.

cache-it.title: Lots of reads, few writes
cache-it.story: 95% of requests read the same hot data. The database is straining.
cache-it.concept: Caching: ElastiCache answers most reads in 1–2 ms so the database can shrink.
cache-it.nudge: Connect EC2 to both ElastiCache and RDS. The cache answers 85% of reads, so RDS Medium is enough.

cache-crash.title: The cache crashes
cache-crash.story: The cache saves a lot, but what if it dies?
cache-crash.concept: Caches need HA too: use a Multi-AZ replica, or keep a database that survives without the cache.
cache-crash.nudge: Turn on Multi-AZ for ElastiCache (or add read replicas to take reads).

static-files.title: Images, images, images
static-files.story: The app is now all images: 85% of 4,000 req/s are static files.
static-files.concept: Do not make servers send static files: store them in S3 and serve them from CloudFront edges.
static-files.nudge: Users → CloudFront; CloudFront → S3 (static) and → ALB → EC2 → RDS (dynamic).

global-users.title: Users all over the world
global-users.story: 70% of users are in Europe, but the system lives in us-east-1. Target: 140 ms or less.
global-users.concept: Distance means latency: bring content to the edge (CloudFront) and ride the AWS backbone (Global Accelerator).
global-users.nudge: Put CloudFront in front of everything, turn on "Cache API responses", use S3 for static files.

background-jobs.title: Emails and PDF exports
background-jobs.story: 30% of requests are heavy jobs: emails and PDF invoices. Users wait 400 ms each time.
background-jobs.concept: Decoupling: push heavy work onto SQS, answer the user right away, let workers do it later.
background-jobs.nudge: Web EC2 → SQS → worker EC2 → RDS. The web tier still talks to RDS for reads and writes.

fan-out.title: One order, many systems
fan-out.story: Every order must reach both email and analytics, and one failing must not take down the other.
fan-out.concept: Fan-out: SNS pushes one message to many SQS queues, each with its own worker.
fan-out.nudge: EC2 → SNS → 2 SQS queues → one EC2 Medium worker each.

lock-it-down.title: Security audit
lock-it-down.story: The auditor opens your board and frowns: the database faces the internet, unencrypted.
lock-it-down.concept: Defense in depth: databases in private subnets, servers behind a load balancer, data encrypted with KMS.
lock-it-down.nudge: Delete the Users → RDS wire, put an ALB in front of EC2, turn on encryption for RDS.

bot-attack.title: Bot attack
bot-attack.story: A botnet fires junk requests at 6× your real traffic.
bot-attack.concept: Block at the edge: WAF filters bots and floods before they reach servers. Buying more servers just pays the attacker.

serverless.title: Side project, thin wallet
serverless.story: Only 20 req/s and a $12/month budget. One EC2 + RDS is already over.
serverless.concept: Serverless: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB on-demand, pay per request, almost $0 when idle.

spot-workers.title: Cheap workers
spot-workers.story: 60% of traffic is image processing. On-Demand workers blow the budget.
spot-workers.concept: Spot is up to 90% cheaper but can be taken back. With SQS, jobs wait in the queue and catch up later.
spot-workers.nudge: Worker EC2 Large ×2 on Spot pricing, fed by SQS.

steady-table.title: Steady traffic
steady-table.story: 2,000 req/s day and night, barely changing. DynamoDB on-demand bills every request.
steady-table.concept: Predictable traffic → provisioned capacity beats on-demand. Unpredictable traffic → on-demand.
steady-table.nudge: Turn on provisioned capacity for DynamoDB, size Large.

reserved.title: Running 24/7 all year
reserved.story: A steady 1,000 req/s that will run all year. The budget got cut.
reserved.concept: A 1–3 year commitment (Reserved Instances / Savings Plans) saves up to ~72% on steady base load.
reserved.nudge: EC2 Medium ×3 on Reserved pricing; add ElastiCache so RDS can stay Medium.

final-boss.title: Global launch day
final-boss.story: Everything at once: global users, images, background jobs, a security audit, and an AZ about to fail.
final-boss.concept: Combine it all: edge, multi-AZ HA, caching, decoupling, encryption and sensible cost.
final-boss.nudge: CloudFront (+S3, API cache) → ALB → EC2 (AZ a+b, ASG) → ElastiCache + RDS (Multi-AZ, encrypted); EC2 → SQS → worker.

short-mvp.title: First version
short-mvp.story: A few friends try it: 30 requests/s, mostly clicks (reads) and the odd new link (write). The budget is only $15/month.
short-mvp.concept: Low, bursty traffic suits serverless: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB on-demand, paid per request.
short-mvp.nudge: Users → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB. One EC2 + RDS already costs $30.

short-viral.title: A link goes viral
short-viral.story: One link is shared everywhere: 1,200 clicks per second, and pay-per-request Lambda is burning money. Every click on the same link returns the same answer.
short-viral.concept: Redirects are cacheable: CloudFront keeps the response at the edge, so most clicks never reach Lambda.
short-viral.nudge: Put CloudFront in front of API Gateway and turn on "Cache API responses".

short-global.title: Clicks from everywhere
short-global.story: 60% of clicks come from Europe. Far-away users wait too long; the target is now under 100 ms.
short-global.concept: CloudFront already answers cacheable clicks at the edge. The rest (new or rare links) needs Global Accelerator to ride the AWS backbone instead of the public internet.
short-global.nudge: Put Global Accelerator between CloudFront and API Gateway.

short-spam.title: Spam bots
short-spam.story: A botnet pumps junk requests at 6× real traffic. Lambda and DynamoDB charge per request, so every junk request costs money.
short-spam.concept: Stop bots at the edge with WAF (rate-based rules) so you never pay for attack traffic.
short-spam.nudge: Put WAF right after Users, in front of CloudFront.

site-1-launch.title: Launch day
site-1-launch.story: The site is only HTML, CSS and images: 300 requests/s, 30% of visitors abroad. Budget $8/month, target under 60 ms.
site-1-launch.concept: Static content needs no servers: store it in S3 and serve it through CloudFront, cached close to users.
site-1-launch.nudge: Users → CloudFront → S3. A single small EC2 already costs $15.

site-2-contact.title: Contact form
site-2-contact.story: Marketing wants a contact form and a post list: 400 requests/s, 15% API reads and 5% form posts. Budget $24.
site-2-contact.concept: A small, bursty dynamic part suits serverless: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB, paid per request.
site-2-contact.nudge: Keep CloudFront → S3 and add CloudFront → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB.

site-3-global.title: Visitors worldwide
site-3-global.story: An international campaign: 800 requests/s, 70% of visitors in Europe, far from us-east-1. The post list is the same for everyone. Target under 55 ms.
site-3-global.concept: CloudFront can also cache read-heavy API responses: half the reads are answered at the edge instead of the Region.
site-3-global.nudge: Turn on "Cache API responses" on CloudFront.

site-4-bots.title: Form spam bots
site-4-bots.story: A botnet pumps junk requests at 6× real traffic into the form. Lambda overloads and API Gateway bills every junk request.
site-4-bots.concept: AWS WAF rate-based rules stop bots at the edge, before they reach (and get billed by) pay-per-request services.
site-4-bots.nudge: Put WAF right after Users, in front of CloudFront.

site-5-encrypt.title: Customer data
site-5-encrypt.story: The form now stores emails and phone numbers; legal requires all data encrypted at rest and only code may reach the database. 1,000 requests/s.
site-5-encrypt.concept: Encryption at rest with KMS: S3 is encrypted by default, but the DynamoDB table must be too. The database stays behind Lambda.
site-5-encrypt.nudge: Turn on encryption on DynamoDB; keep DynamoDB connected only from Lambda.

site-6-squeeze.title: Cost squeeze
site-6-squeeze.story: Traffic has settled at 1,600 requests/s with lots of newsletter sign-ups (writes). The boss cuts the budget to $68.
site-6-squeeze.concept: Steady, predictable traffic is cheaper on DynamoDB provisioned capacity than on-demand, which bills every request.
site-6-squeeze.nudge: Turn on provisioned capacity on DynamoDB; size Small is enough.

notif-1-mvp.title: Pilot
notif-1-mvp.story: 40 requests/s: notification history (reads), settings (writes) and 30% send commands. Budget $7; waiting up to 250 ms is fine.
notif-1-mvp.concept: At low traffic serverless is cheapest: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB, no server running all day.
notif-1-mvp.nudge: Users → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB. Lambda can send the notifications itself for now.

notif-2-queue.title: Sending is slow
notif-2-queue.story: Other teams start calling the API: 250 requests/s. Sending inside the request adds 400 ms to every command; the target is now under 100 ms.
notif-2-queue.concept: Take sending out of the request: Lambda drops the command into SQS and answers at once; a worker reads the queue and sends later.
notif-2-queue.nudge: Connect Lambda → SQS → a Medium EC2 worker.

notif-3-fanout.title: Three channels
notif-3-fanout.story: Every command must now go out as push, email and SMS. A slow channel must not hold up the others, and no command may be lost. 300 requests/s.
notif-3-fanout.concept: SNS fan-out: Lambda publishes one message to a topic; SNS copies it into three SQS queues, one worker per channel.
notif-3-fanout.nudge: Lambda → SNS → three SQS queues (Push, Email, SMS), each with a Medium EC2 worker.

notif-4-sale.title: Flash sale
notif-4-sale.story: A big customer runs a flash sale: 3× traffic for almost a third of the day. Every notification must still be sent by the end of the day.
notif-4-sale.concept: SQS absorbs the burst; Auto Scaling adds workers while they are busy so the queues drain in time.
notif-4-sale.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling for all three EC2 workers.

notif-5-lambda.title: Pay per message
notif-5-lambda.story: Outside the flash sale, the EC2 workers sit idle most of the time. The budget is cut to $95.
notif-5-lambda.concept: Bursty workers suit Lambda: SQS triggers Lambda, which scales on its own and bills only for the messages it processes.
notif-5-lambda.nudge: Replace the three EC2 workers with three Lambdas reading the three SQS queues.

notif-6-encrypt.title: Emails and phone numbers
notif-6-encrypt.story: Queued messages hold customer emails and phone numbers; the auditor requires all data encrypted at rest. Traffic grows to 450 requests/s.
notif-6-encrypt.concept: Encryption at rest with KMS everywhere data is stored: the SQS queues as well as the DynamoDB table.
notif-6-encrypt.nudge: Turn on encryption on DynamoDB and all three SQS queues.

sapi-launch.title: Launch day
sapi-launch.story: The API just went live: about 80 requests/s, 70% reads and 30% writes. Money is tight: $15/month.
sapi-launch.concept: Small, uneven traffic suits serverless: API Gateway + Lambda + on-demand DynamoDB bill per request, with no idle servers to pay for.
sapi-launch.nudge: Users → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB. A small EC2 + RDS already costs $30.

sapi-growth.title: Steady traffic
sapi-growth.story: Customers arrive: 900 requests/s around the clock. The serverless bill is past $130 and the budget is $120.
sapi-growth.concept: Per-request pricing grows linearly with traffic. Under high, steady load, EC2 behind an ALB plus provisioned DynamoDB (flat price) beats Lambda and on-demand DynamoDB.
sapi-growth.nudge: Replace API Gateway + Lambda with ALB → one large EC2, and switch DynamoDB to provisioned (medium).

sapi-az.title: An AZ goes down
sapi-az.story: Business customers want an uptime promise. That same week an AZ fails, and the only server lives in it.
sapi-az.concept: Multi-AZ: run at least two servers in two AZs behind the ALB. Each AZ must carry all 900 requests/s alone when the other is gone. DynamoDB already replicates across AZs.
sapi-az.nudge: Set EC2 to 2 large instances in "AZ a+b".

sapi-cache.title: More reads than writes
sapi-cache.story: A mobile app joins: 2,000 requests/s, 90% re-reading the same data. The medium DynamoDB table is overloaded, and a large one blows the $200 budget.
sapi-cache.concept: ElastiCache in front of the database keeps hot data in memory: about 85% of reads never touch DynamoDB, so a small table is enough.
sapi-cache.nudge: Add a small ElastiCache and connect EC2 → ElastiCache; keep EC2 → DynamoDB for writes and cache misses.

sapi-reserved.title: Cut the bill
sapi-reserved.story: Investors want the bill under $145/month. Load is still 2,000 requests/s, steady 24/7. Someone suggests Spot, but AWS can reclaim Spot at any moment.
sapi-reserved.concept: Steady, long-running base load belongs on Reserved Instances (or Savings Plans): about 40% cheaper and never reclaimed like Spot. Spot is only for work that tolerates interruption.
sapi-reserved.nudge: Switch the EC2 pricing to Reserved. Do not run the API on Spot.

sapi-peak.title: Promo campaign
sapi-peak.story: A normal day is 1,000 requests/s, but a promo triples traffic for a few hours. Budget: $195.
sapi-peak.concept: Mix pricing models: Reserved for the base load that is always there, Auto Scaling adds on-demand instances for short peaks. Reserving for the peak pays for idle servers.
sapi-peak.nudge: Keep 2 Reserved instances as the base and turn on Auto Scaling for EC2 (max 4).

vault-share.title: Share without going public
vault-share.story: The company needs a place to share contracts and reports: 400 requests/s, 70% file downloads, the rest listing files and permissions. Last year a public bucket leaked customer contracts: this time no bucket may be open to the internet.
vault-share.concept: Turn on S3 Block Public Access for the account and encrypt with SSE-KMS. CloudFront reads the bucket through Origin Access Control; API Gateway + Lambda checks permissions and issues short-lived signed URLs. Staff sign in through Cognito or IAM Identity Center instead of sharing keys.
vault-share.nudge: Users → CloudFront; CloudFront → S3 for files and CloudFront → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB (encrypted).

vault-scan.title: Scan uploads for viruses
vault-scan.story: Staff start uploading files: 15% of requests are new files that need a virus scan, and each scan takes a few hundred ms. Scanning inside the request slows the whole app, and unscanned files may not be shared.
vault-scan.concept: Lambda stores the file as pending and sends a job to an encrypted SQS; another Lambda scans it and marks it clean. On AWS, GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 can also scan new files without custom code.
vault-scan.nudge: Add an encrypted SQS fed by Lambda, and a second Lambda reading from it.

vault-scrape.title: Scraping bots
vault-scrape.story: A botnet uses leaked accounts to scrape documents in bulk at 6× real traffic. Lambda is swamped and real staff cannot open files. Security requires every request to pass through WAF.
vault-scrape.concept: WAF on CloudFront blocks at the edge, before the API: rate-based rules, Bot Control, and geo match if the company only works in a few countries. GuardDuty spots credentials used in unusual ways so the account can be locked in time.
vault-scrape.nudge: Put WAF between Users and CloudFront.

vault-region.title: A whole Region fails
vault-region.story: us-east-1 has a major outage for a few hours. Contracts must still open, and the European office (40% of users) needs speed. Copies in another Region must follow the same security rules as the original.
vault-region.concept: S3 Cross-Region Replication to eu-west-1, with the target bucket encrypted and Block Public Access on; a KMS multi-Region key lets both Regions decrypt with the same key. A DynamoDB global table keeps data in both Regions, and Route 53 sends requests to the Region still alive.
vault-region.nudge: Add a second S3 in eu-west-1 behind CloudFront; CloudFront → Route 53 → API Gateway + Lambda + SQS in each Region, and turn on Global for DynamoDB.

photo-1-launch.title: Fast photo views
photo-1-launch.story: 600 requests/s, 75% are image downloads, the rest are feed reads and new photos (writes). 20% of users are in Europe. Target under 80 ms.
photo-1-launch.concept: Images are static content: keep them in S3 and serve them through CloudFront. App servers only handle the API.
photo-1-launch.nudge: CloudFront → S3 for images, CloudFront → ALB → EC2 → RDS for the API.

photo-2-thumbs.title: Thumbnails
photo-2-thumbs.story: Every new photo needs thumbnails: 10% of requests are heavy jobs. Done inside the app server, users wait 400 ms more. 800 requests/s, target under 75 ms.
photo-2-thumbs.concept: Move heavy work out of the request: the server drops a job into SQS and answers at once; a separate worker does it later.
photo-2-thumbs.nudge: Connect app EC2 → SQS → a Medium EC2 worker.

photo-3-fanout.title: Notify followers
photo-3-fanout.story: For every new photo, besides thumbnails, every follower’s feed must be updated. Two independent jobs; neither may wait for the other. 1,000 requests/s.
photo-3-fanout.concept: SNS fan-out: one message published to a topic is copied into several SQS queues, each with its own worker.
photo-3-fanout.nudge: App EC2 → SNS → two SQS queues (thumbnails, feed), each with an EC2 worker.

photo-4-spot.title: Cheap workers
photo-4-spot.story: Traffic stays the same but the budget is cut to $130. Workers process queued jobs; a few seconds of delay is fine.
photo-4-spot.concept: Background work that tolerates interruption is the ideal fit for Spot Instances: up to 70% cheaper than On-Demand.
photo-4-spot.nudge: Switch both EC2 workers to Spot pricing.

photo-5-interrupt.title: Spot reclaimed
photo-5-interrupt.story: Midday, AWS reclaims every Spot instance for a while. Jobs pile up in the queues and must all be done by the end of the day.
photo-5-interrupt.concept: Spot can be reclaimed at any time. SQS keeps the jobs safe, but workers need spare capacity to drain the backlog once they return.
photo-5-interrupt.nudge: Grow the Spot workers to size Large so they have room to drain the queues.

photo-6-viral.title: A photo goes viral
photo-6-viral.story: One photo spreads everywhere: traffic climbs from 1,000 to 4,000 requests/s during the day. Feed reads surge and background jobs grow with them.
photo-6-viral.concept: Auto Scaling for both app servers and workers, plus ElastiCache and CloudFront caching so the database does not take every read.
photo-6-viral.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling for the app EC2 and the workers, add ElastiCache behind the app EC2, and turn on "Cache API responses".

shop-1-mvp.title: Open the shop
shop-1-mvp.story: A handmade-goods shop opens: 250 requests/s, 80% browsing products (reads) and 20% carts and orders (writes). Budget $70/month.
shop-1-mvp.concept: The basic setup: EC2 servers run the code, RDS stores the data. Size each for its load, and remember a write costs RDS three times as much as a read.
shop-1-mvp.nudge: Users → EC2 → RDS. Small is too small for both: try Medium.

shop-2-scale-out.title: Scale out
shop-2-scale-out.story: The shop gets press: 1,200 requests/s. A Large server handles exactly 1,200 units/s before traffic even wobbles. Budget $178/month.
shop-2-scale-out.concept: Scale out instead of up: put an ALB in front and spread the load over several smaller EC2 instances. A few Medium servers cost less than one XLarge and stop being a single point of failure.
shop-2-scale-out.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 Medium ×3 → RDS Large.

shop-3-az-outage.title: Losing an AZ
shop-3-az-outage.story: Still 1,200 requests/s, but today us-east-1a loses power for almost half the round, and every server and the database live in AZ a. Budget $320/month.
shop-3-az-outage.concept: High availability: spread EC2 over 2 AZs in an Auto Scaling Group so it replaces dead instances in the surviving AZ, and turn on RDS Multi-AZ for automatic failover.
shop-3-az-outage.nudge: EC2 Medium ×4, AZ "AZ a+b", Auto Scaling Group on (max 4). RDS Large with Multi-AZ.

shop-4-catalog-cache.title: Cache the catalog
shop-4-catalog-cache.story: Holiday season: 2,000 requests/s, 95% browsing the catalog and product pages, the same data read over and over. Making RDS carry it all takes XLarge with Multi-AZ, far over the $230/month budget.
shop-4-catalog-cache.concept: Read-heavy, rarely changing data belongs in a cache: ElastiCache answers ~85% of reads in a few ms, so RDS only sees cache misses and writes.
shop-4-catalog-cache.nudge: Connect EC2 → ElastiCache and keep EC2 → RDS. RDS can now be Medium; use 2 Large EC2 instances.

shop-5-flash-sale.title: Midnight flash sale
shop-5-flash-sale.story: Normally 2,000 requests/s; the midnight flash sale triples it for about a third of the round. Keeping enough servers for the peak all day blows the $480/month budget.
shop-5-flash-sale.concept: An Auto Scaling Group with target tracking adds instances when load passes ~60% and removes them after the sale. The cache and database do not scale by themselves, so size them for the peak.
shop-5-flash-sale.nudge: EC2 Large, min 3, max 8, Auto Scaling Group on. ElastiCache Medium, RDS Large.

shop-6-launch-day.title: Launch day
shop-6-launch-day.story: The new collection launches: 2,000 requests/s, a 3× flash sale, and 20% of requests are orders (payment, stock, emails) that take 400 ms each when done inline. The target is under 150 ms, and every order must be processed before the round ends.
shop-6-launch-day.concept: Take order processing out of the web path: the web tier puts orders on SQS and answers at once, and workers process them at their own pace. The queue absorbs the sale peak, so workers need not be peak-sized.
shop-6-launch-day.nudge: Web EC2 → SQS → worker EC2 (one XLarge is enough to drain the queue after the sale). Keep web → ElastiCache and RDS.

tix-1-on-sale.title: A small show goes on sale
tix-1-on-sale.story: A 2,000-seat show: normally 200 requests/s (60% browsing seats, 40% booking), tripling when sales open. Budget $140/month.
tix-1-on-sale.concept: An Auto Scaling Group lets the web tier follow the on-sale rush and shrink afterwards. The database does not scale by itself, so size it for the peak; each write costs RDS three reads.
tix-1-on-sale.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 Medium (Auto Scaling Group on, max 4) → RDS Large.

tix-2-write-behind.title: Queue the bookings
tix-2-write-behind.story: A stadium show: 900 requests/s, 60% of them bookings. When sales open, writes triple and overwhelm even an XLarge RDS. Averaged over the round, though, XLarge keeps up. Budget $460/month.
tix-2-write-behind.concept: Write-behind: web servers do not write to the database; they put bookings on SQS and workers write them to RDS at a steady pace. Reads go through ElastiCache, and only misses reach RDS. The queue turns a sharp spike into a steady stream.
tix-2-write-behind.nudge: Remove web EC2 → RDS. Connect web → ElastiCache → RDS (reads) and web → SQS → worker EC2 (Medium ×3) → RDS (writes).

tix-3-dynamodb.title: Move to DynamoDB
tix-3-dynamodb.story: A national tour: 2,000 requests/s, still 60% bookings, 3× when sales open. Even with the queue, the average write rate is more than the biggest RDS can take. Budget $650/month.
tix-3-dynamodb.concept: DynamoDB scales out almost without limit. Pick the capacity mode by the shape of the load: on-demand for unpredictable load, provisioned for steady load at a much lower price. Workers behind a queue are exactly that steady load.
tix-3-dynamodb.nudge: Replace RDS with DynamoDB and turn on Provisioned capacity, Large. Worker: one XLarge instance. Web EC2 Large, min 2, max 8.

tix-4-bots.title: Scalper bots
tix-4-bots.story: Scalpers aim a botnet at the sale, sending 6× the real traffic to grab tickets. The web servers drown and real fans cannot buy.
tix-4-bots.concept: AWS WAF rate-based rules stop bots at the edge, before they reach the ALB and the servers. Much cheaper than adding servers to absorb junk traffic.
tix-4-bots.nudge: Put WAF right after Users, in front of the ALB.

tix-5-e-tickets.title: Sending e-tickets
tix-5-e-tickets.story: Every ticket sold needs a QR e-ticket generated and emailed: 40% of requests are now heavy jobs on the queue. One worker cannot keep up, and every ticket must go out before the round ends.
tix-5-e-tickets.concept: Workers need to scale too: a heavy job costs a worker three times a write. An Auto Scaling Group for workers adds instances when the queue backs up (in practice, scale on SQS queue depth).
tix-5-e-tickets.nudge: Switch the worker to Large, min 2, max 4, with the Auto Scaling Group on.

tix-6-world-tour.title: World tour
tix-6-world-tour.story: A world tour: 2,000 requests/s, 60% of fans in Europe, 3× when sales open. A quarter of requests download seat maps (static files). The target is under 100 ms.
tix-6-world-tour.concept: CloudFront serves static files from S3 at an edge near each fan and carries the rest to the origin over the faster AWS network. The web servers no longer serve static files.
tix-6-world-tour.nudge: Add CloudFront after WAF: connect CloudFront → S3 (seat maps) and CloudFront → ALB.

feed-1-launch.title: Feed launch
feed-1-launch.story: 800 requests/s: 90% scrolling the feed (reads), 10% posting and liking (writes). Budget $150/month.
feed-1-launch.concept: A read-heavy app: scale the web tier out behind an ALB, and size the database for reads plus writes (a write costs RDS three reads).
feed-1-launch.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 Medium ×2 → RDS Large.

feed-2-read-replica.title: Replicas for reads
feed-2-read-replica.story: Still 800 requests/s, but one AZ is about to lose power for almost half the round. Multi-AZ on a Large RDS doubles its price and breaks the $275/month budget, and the Multi-AZ standby serves no reads.
feed-2-read-replica.concept: Multi-AZ to survive, read replicas to scale reads: keep a Medium primary with Multi-AZ and add a Read Replica in AZ b to take part of the reads. A replica does not double the price like Multi-AZ does.
feed-2-read-replica.nudge: EC2 Medium ×4, "AZ a+b", Auto Scaling Group on (max 4). RDS Medium with Multi-AZ plus a Medium Read Replica in AZ b; connect EC2 to both.

feed-3-cache.title: Cache the feed
feed-3-cache.story: The app takes off: 2,500 requests/s, 95% reads. Adding Large replicas to carry every read blows the $330/month budget.
feed-3-cache.concept: Each person's feed is read again and again: ElastiCache answers ~85% of reads, so the database and replica only see misses and writes. A cache is far cheaper than more replicas.
feed-3-cache.nudge: Add a Small ElastiCache and connect EC2 → ElastiCache. Switch EC2 to Large ×3.

feed-4-cache-crash.title: The cache crashes
feed-4-cache-crash.story: The only ElastiCache node dies mid-round. All 2,500 requests/s land on the database and replica, which were sized for cache misses only.
feed-4-cache-crash.concept: A cache is a point of failure too. ElastiCache Multi-AZ keeps a replica in another AZ that takes over at once, much cheaper than a database big enough to serve every read.

feed-5-viral.title: A post goes viral
feed-5-viral.story: A post goes viral: traffic climbs steadily from 1,500 to 6,000 requests/s over the round. A fixed fleet cannot keep up, and sizing for the end of the round is wasteful. Budget $680/month.
feed-5-viral.concept: Auto Scaling lets the web tier follow growing traffic. The cache and database do not scale by themselves: move ElastiCache to Medium and the RDS primary to Large to cope with the end of the round.
feed-5-viral.nudge: EC2 Large, min 2, max 8, Auto Scaling Group on. ElastiCache Medium (Multi-AZ), RDS Large (Multi-AZ).

feed-6-global.title: Readers worldwide
feed-6-global.story: The app goes international: 3,000 requests/s, 60% of users in Europe. They wait too long: the target is now under 120 ms, and the budget is down to $550/month.
feed-6-global.concept: CloudFront can cache API responses too: hot feeds are served at an edge near the reader, and the rest travels to the origin over the AWS network. Faster for far-away users, and less load on EC2, so fewer servers.
feed-6-global.nudge: Put CloudFront between Users and the ALB and turn on "Cache API responses".

ehr-private.title: Medical data is sensitive
ehr-private.story: The clinic chain puts health records online: 300 requests/s, 70% doctors and patients reading records, 30% updates. Health data rules demand: encrypt all data, keep the database private, and no server may take connections straight from the internet.
ehr-private.concept: Three tiers inside a VPC: the ALB in a public subnet, EC2 and RDS in private subnets. The RDS security group only allows port 5432 from the EC2 security group. RDS encrypts at rest with a KMS key, and it must be turned on at creation: a running database cannot be encrypted in place.
ehr-private.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 (medium) → RDS (medium), with encryption on for RDS.

ehr-scans.title: X-ray images
ehr-scans.story: Patients can now view X-rays and lab results: traffic grows to 700 requests/s, nearly half of them file downloads. Serving files from EC2 overloads the servers. Security bans public buckets: anyone holding a link could download patient data.
ehr-scans.concept: Store files in S3 with Block Public Access on, and serve them through CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC): the bucket policy only lets CloudFront read. To let only the right patient download, the app issues short-lived signed URLs or signed cookies.
ehr-scans.nudge: Users → CloudFront; CloudFront → S3 for files and CloudFront → ALB for the rest.

ehr-cache.title: Doctors need fast lookups
ehr-cache.story: In the clinic, doctors open records all day: 900 requests/s, mostly re-reading the same records. RDS cannot keep up and the latency target drops to 70 ms. Health data in a cache is still health data.
ehr-cache.concept: ElastiCache takes repeated reads off RDS. Turn on encryption at rest and in transit (TLS) for the cache, add a Redis AUTH token or RBAC users, and keep the cache in a private subnet that only EC2 can reach.
ehr-cache.nudge: Add ElastiCache linked from EC2 and turn on its encryption.

ehr-stuffing.title: Credential stuffing
ehr-stuffing.story: Attackers try millions of email/password pairs leaked from other sites (credential stuffing), hitting the portal at 6× real traffic. Auditors also require every request to pass a web application firewall before it reaches a server.
ehr-stuffing.concept: Attach AWS WAF to CloudFront: a rate-based rule caps logins per IP, and the Account Takeover Prevention and Bot Control managed rules stop bots. Shield Standard covers the network layer for free; Shield Advanced adds a DDoS response team and cost protection.
ehr-stuffing.nudge: Put WAF between Users and CloudFront.

ehr-audit.title: Record access log
ehr-audit.story: The law requires logging who viewed which record and sending patients an access report on request: 15% of requests build a report, each taking a few hundred ms. No report may be lost, and the queue holds patient data too.
ehr-audit.concept: Send report jobs to SQS with SSE-KMS, and let a separate worker build them. CloudTrail records every AWS API call; turn on CloudTrail log file validation and store logs in S3 with Object Lock so nobody can change them.
ehr-audit.nudge: Add an encrypted SQS fed by the web EC2, and a medium EC2 worker reading from it.

vid-1-launch.title: First course goes live
vid-1-launch.story: 2,000 requests/s: 85% video segments and images, 12% lesson lists, 3% progress saves. Half the students are in Europe, far from us-east-1. Target under 110 ms, budget $115/month.
vid-1-launch.concept: Static content lives in S3 and CloudFront serves it from an edge near each student: servers stop carrying video and far users skip the ~150 ms trip.
vid-1-launch.nudge: Users → CloudFront. CloudFront → S3 for video, and CloudFront → ALB → EC2 → RDS for the rest.

vid-2-transcode.title: Instructors upload videos
vid-2-transcode.story: Traffic grows to 2,500 requests/s and 5% are new videos to transcode into several resolutions. Transcoding inside the web servers adds 400 ms and triples the work. Every job must be done by the end of the round.
vid-2-transcode.concept: Move heavy work off the request path: the web tier drops a job into SQS and answers at once, a separate worker fleet pulls jobs and transcodes.
vid-2-transcode.nudge: Connect the web server → SQS → a separate EC2 worker (Medium is enough).

vid-3-spot.title: Cheaper transcoding
vid-3-spot.story: The budget drops to $135/month. Transcoding is not urgent, a few minutes late is fine, but AWS can reclaim Spot instances mid-round. The queue must still be empty at the end.
vid-3-spot.concept: Queue workers are a perfect fit for Spot (~70% cheaper): when instances are reclaimed, jobs wait safely in SQS. You just need spare capacity to catch up afterwards.
vid-3-spot.nudge: Switch the worker to Spot and size it up to Large so it can clear the backlog after the interruption.

vid-4-catalog.title: Enrollment season
vid-4-catalog.story: 4,000 requests/s and students browse the catalog more: 20% are reads. RDS and the web tier are overloaded, the target tightens to 100 ms, budget $200/month.
vid-4-catalog.concept: The course catalog looks the same for everyone: cache it at the edge with CloudFront and in the Region with ElastiCache so most reads never reach the database.
vid-4-catalog.nudge: Turn on "Cache API responses" on CloudFront, add ElastiCache next to RDS, and run 2 Medium web servers.

vid-5-region.title: A whole Region goes down
vid-5-region.story: us-east-1 loses power for almost half the round. Its S3, ALB, EC2 and RDS all die, leaving CloudFront with no origin. Half the students are still in Europe. Budget $330/month.
vid-5-region.concept: Build a second stack in eu-west-1 (S3, ALB, EC2, database) and put Route 53 behind CloudFront: health checks fail over to the live Region and latency routing sends European students to the closer one.
vid-5-region.nudge: CloudFront → Route 53 → S3 + ALB in both Regions. In eu-west-1: ALB → 2 Medium EC2. Replace RDS with a Small Aurora, turn on Aurora Global Database and link the EC2 in both Regions to it.

vid-6-sale.title: Big sale day
vid-6-sale.story: The year-end sale triples traffic for a few minutes mid-round, in both Regions. Keeping enough servers for the peak all day blows the $440/month budget.
vid-6-sale.concept: An Auto Scaling Group adds instances as load rises and removes them afterwards, so you only pay for the peak while it lasts.
vid-6-sale.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling Group (max 5) for the web servers in both Regions.

dr-1-launch.title: First customers
dr-1-launch.story: Three companies start a trial: 300 requests/s, 80% dashboard reads, 20% writes. Budget $90/month.
dr-1-launch.concept: A basic three-tier design: an ALB in front of EC2, data in RDS. The ALB is a stable entry point you can add servers behind later.
dr-1-launch.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 (Medium) → RDS (Medium). A Small RDS cannot keep up with the writes.

dr-2-az.title: A contract with an SLA
dr-2-az.story: A big customer signs a 99.9% SLA. Traffic is 350 requests/s, and one AZ loses power mid-round. Budget $155/month.
dr-2-az.concept: High availability inside a Region: EC2 spread over two AZs behind the ALB, and RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby that takes over when the primary AZ dies.
dr-2-az.nudge: Run 2 EC2 in "AZ a+b" and turn on Multi-AZ for RDS.

dr-3-region.title: A DR plan
dr-3-region.story: The auditor asks: what if all of us-east-1 goes down? This round it is dead for almost half the time. Budget $250/month, target under 150 ms.
dr-3-region.concept: Warm standby: a scaled-down copy of the system always runs in another Region (eu-west-1). The database is an Aurora Global Database: AWS keeps a copy in eu-west-1 (~1 s behind) and fails over to it in ~1 minute when the primary Region is lost, with no manual promotion as with a cross-Region RDS replica. Route 53 failover uses health checks to move users to eu-west-1, then Auto Scaling grows it to full size.
dr-3-region.nudge: Users → Route 53 → an ALB in each Region. In eu-west-1: ALB → 1 Medium EC2 with Auto Scaling Group (max 3). Replace RDS with a Small Aurora, turn on Aurora Global Database, and link the EC2 in both Regions to Aurora.

dr-4-comply.title: Compliance audit
dr-4-comply.story: A bank wants to sign, with conditions: all data encrypted at rest, no exposed database, no server taking requests straight from the internet. us-east-1 can still go down.
dr-4-comply.concept: KMS encryption at rest must cover every data store; with Aurora Global Database the copy in eu-west-1 uses a KMS key in that Region. Databases are reachable only from the app tier, and EC2 sits behind the ALB in private subnets.
dr-4-comply.nudge: Turn on "Encryption at rest (KMS)" for Aurora.

dr-5-active.title: European customers
dr-5-active.story: Traffic grows to 1,000 requests/s, 40% from Europe, and the target tightens to 120 ms. Route 53 sends them to eu-west-1, which is closer, so the scaled-down copy is overloaded even without an outage.
dr-5-active.concept: From warm standby to active-active: Route 53 latency routing serves each user from the nearest Region, so both Regions need real capacity. An encrypted ElastiCache in each Region takes reads off the database.
dr-5-active.nudge: Give both Regions 2 Medium EC2 with Auto Scaling Group (max 4), and add an encrypted ElastiCache in each Region.

dr-6-reserved.title: Trim the bill
dr-6-reserved.story: Finance wants the bill down to $280/month without giving up a Region. The base servers run 24/7 and will for years.
dr-6-reserved.concept: Steady, long-lived base load should be Reserved (~40% cheaper), while the extra Auto Scaling instances at peak stay On-Demand. Spot does not suit a customer-facing web tier because it can be reclaimed at any time.
dr-6-reserved.nudge: Switch the EC2 pricing in both Regions to Reserved.

iot-1-pilot.title: Pilot
iot-1-pilot.story: A few hundred sensors in one factory send 200 readings/s, all writes. Budget $45/month.
iot-1-pilot.concept: Each reading is a small item keyed by device and time: a natural fit for DynamoDB. At low load, API Gateway + Lambda + on-demand DynamoDB is cheap and serverless.
iot-1-pilot.nudge: Users → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB. A Small RDS cannot take 200 writes/s.

iot-2-steady.title: Steady stream
iot-2-steady.story: The whole factory chain is online: 1,500 writes/s, steady day and night. One Lambda cannot keep up, and paying per request on DynamoDB is now too expensive. Budget $250/month.
iot-2-steady.concept: For steady, predictable traffic, DynamoDB provisioned capacity (a fixed price per WCU/RCU) is much cheaper than on-demand.
iot-2-steady.nudge: ALB → 2 Large EC2 → DynamoDB with Provisioned capacity, size Large.

iot-3-storm.title: Reconnect storm
iot-3-storm.story: After a firmware update every device reconnects at once and replays its data: traffic triples for a few minutes. Sizing the database for the peak blows the $400/month budget.
iot-3-storm.concept: Use SQS as a buffer: API Gateway writes straight into the queue and workers pull at the pace the database can take. The spike is spread out over time and the database keeps its size.
iot-3-storm.nudge: Users → API Gateway → SQS → 3 Large EC2 workers → DynamoDB (Provisioned, Large).

iot-4-growth.title: Rapid growth
iot-4-growth.story: New contracts bring devices online every day: traffic climbs from 1,500 to 6,000 writes/s during the round. The queue must be empty at the end; no reading may wait forever.
iot-4-growth.concept: A queue postpones work, it does not remove it. When load keeps growing, the worker fleet must grow with it (Auto Scaling) and the database must fit the final write rate.
iot-4-growth.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling Group for the workers (2 instances, max 5) and size DynamoDB up to XLarge.

iot-5-dash.title: Customer dashboards
iot-5-dash.story: Traffic settles at 5,000 requests/s: 60% sensor readings, 40% customers opening dashboards with the latest numbers. Reading straight from DynamoDB needs an XLarge table and blows the $720/month budget.
iot-5-dash.concept: Dashboards read the same numbers again and again: ElastiCache answers most reads in a few ms and DynamoDB only sees the misses, so the table stays smaller.
iot-5-dash.nudge: API Gateway → ALB → 2 Large EC2 for dashboards → ElastiCache → DynamoDB. Connect the dashboard servers to SQS too. Workers: 4 Large EC2; DynamoDB Provisioned, Large.

iot-6-cache-crash.title: The cache fails
iot-6-cache-crash.story: The ElastiCache node dies mid-round. Without the cache, every dashboard load either fails or lands on DynamoDB.
iot-6-cache-crash.concept: A cache is a single point of failure too. ElastiCache Multi-AZ keeps a replica in another AZ that takes over when the primary node dies, so dashboards keep working.

lb-hot.title: Hot leaderboard
lb-hot.story: The game just launched: 2,500 requests/s, 92% opening the leaderboard and 8% posting scores. Everyone looks at the same top 100. Budget: $260.
lb-hot.concept: Constantly read data like a leaderboard belongs in ElastiCache (Redis sorted sets). The cache serves most reads, so DynamoDB only takes writes and cache misses.
lb-hot.nudge: Add ElastiCache next to EC2, then switch DynamoDB to provisioned (medium) instead of paying per request.

lb-global.title: Players everywhere
lb-global.story: The game tops the charts in Europe: 60% of players are far from us-east-1. Gamers complain about lag; the target is now under 80 ms.
lb-global.concept: CloudFront caches API responses (a leaderboard that changes every second still caches well for a moment) at the edge. The rest, like score posts, rides the AWS backbone through Global Accelerator.
lb-global.nudge: Users → CloudFront ("Cache API responses" on) → Global Accelerator → ALB. The edge takes reads off the servers, so 2 EC2 instances are enough.

lb-ddos.title: Bots crash the tournament
lb-ddos.story: Mid-tournament, a botnet floods junk requests at 6× real traffic to take the game servers down. CloudFront bills the junk too.
lb-ddos.concept: AWS WAF with rate-based rules blocks bots at the edge, before they reach CloudFront and EC2. Shield Standard already covers network-layer floods; WAF handles the application layer.
lb-ddos.nudge: Put WAF right after Users, in front of CloudFront.

lb-cachecrash.title: Cache dies mid-season
lb-cachecrash.story: New season: 3,600 requests/s. Mid-match, the only ElastiCache node dies. Every read falls through to DynamoDB and the table is overloaded.
lb-cachecrash.concept: ElastiCache Multi-AZ keeps a replica in another AZ and fails over automatically, so the cache never disappears. Much cheaper than sizing DynamoDB for a cache outage.
lb-cachecrash.nudge: Turn on Multi-AZ for ElastiCache and raise EC2 to 3 large instances for the new traffic.

lb-region.title: A whole Region fails
lb-region.story: A major incident takes us-east-1 down for hours. 60% of players are still far away, so a second Region near them also cuts latency.
lb-region.concept: Multi-Region active-active: one ALB + EC2 + ElastiCache stack per Region, sharing one DynamoDB global table that has a copy in both Regions and takes writes in either. Route 53 sends players to the nearest Region and moves everyone to the surviving one when a Region fails.
lb-region.nudge: Add Route 53 after Global Accelerator, build a second stack in eu-west-1 (2 large EC2 per side is enough) and point Route 53 at both ALBs. Turn on Global Tables for DynamoDB and link the EC2 in both Regions to it.

lb-finals.title: World finals
lb-finals.story: The final is livestreamed: traffic triples for a few hours, then drops back to 3,600 requests/s. The $650 budget cannot run peak capacity all night.
lb-finals.concept: Auto Scaling in each Region adds instances as load rises and removes them after the peak. eu-west-1 serves 60% of players, so it gets more room to grow.
lb-finals.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling for EC2 in both Regions (max 5 and 6).

bank-secure.title: Day-one audit
bank-secure.story: The bank opens its online portal: 400 requests/s, 70% checking balances and history, 30% transfers. Compliance demands from day one: encrypt all data, keep the database private, and no server may take connections straight from the internet.
bank-secure.concept: Defense in depth: only the ALB sits in a public subnet; EC2 and RDS live in private subnets and accept traffic only from the layer in front (security groups). RDS encrypts at rest with KMS.
bank-secure.nudge: Users → ALB → EC2 (medium) → RDS (medium), and turn on encryption for RDS.

bank-az.title: An AZ loses power
bank-az.story: An AZ loses power during business hours. The banking portal must not stop: one server and one database in the same AZ is not enough.
bank-az.concept: Multi-AZ on both tiers: EC2 across two AZs behind the ALB, and RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover.
bank-az.nudge: Set EC2 to 2 instances in "AZ a+b", then turn on Multi-AZ for RDS.

bank-attack.title: Login attack
bank-attack.story: A botnet hammers the login page with junk at 6× real traffic. The ALB forwards it all to EC2, and real customers cannot get in.
bank-attack.concept: AWS WAF in front of the ALB filters application-layer traffic: rate-based rules plus managed rules against SQL injection and bots. Blocked requests never reach the servers.
bank-attack.nudge: Put WAF between Users and the ALB.

bank-statements.title: PDF statements
bank-statements.story: Customers can download PDF statements: 15% of requests create one, and each takes a few hundred ms. Doing it inside the request pushes the whole portal past 120 ms, and no statement may be lost.
bank-statements.concept: Move heavy work off the web path: EC2 sends jobs to SQS (encrypted), and a separate worker pulls them. The web tier answers at once while the queue holds jobs until they are done.
bank-statements.nudge: Add an encrypted SQS fed by EC2, and a small EC2 worker reading from SQS.

bank-far.title: Customers abroad
bank-far.story: The bank opens international branches: 600 requests/s, 40% from customers in Europe, far from us-east-1. A third of requests are static page files (JS, CSS, logos). The latency target is 80 ms.
bank-far.concept: CloudFront serves static files from S3 at the edge. Account data is private, so it is not cached; Global Accelerator instead brings those requests onto the AWS backbone close to the customer.
bank-far.nudge: WAF → CloudFront (API caching off) → S3 for static files, and CloudFront → Global Accelerator → ALB for the rest.

bank-payday.title: Payday
bank-payday.story: On payday, traffic triples for a few hours: everyone checks balances, sends money and downloads statements. The $320 budget cannot run payday capacity all month.
bank-payday.concept: Auto Scaling adds web instances as load rises and removes them after the peak. What does not scale on its own (RDS, the worker) must be sized for the peak.
bank-payday.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling for the web EC2 (max 6), raise RDS to large and the worker to medium.

pay-launch.title: First transactions
pay-launch.story: A digital wallet opens a payment API to merchants: 300 requests/s, half creating payments and half checking status. The team wants serverless so nobody runs servers. PCI DSS requires card data to be encrypted at rest.
pay-launch.concept: API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB. Lambda gets least privilege through its IAM execution role (only PutItem/GetItem on that one table). DynamoDB encrypts with a KMS key; use a customer managed key when you need your own rotation and a CloudTrail record of who used the key.
pay-launch.nudge: Users → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB, with encryption on for DynamoDB.

pay-card-testing.title: Card-testing bots
pay-card-testing.story: Fraudsters use the API to test stolen card numbers in bulk (card testing): junk requests jump 6×. Lambda concurrency runs out and real payments are declined. PCI DSS also requires a web application firewall in front of every public API.
pay-card-testing.concept: Attach AWS WAF to API Gateway: IP rate-based rules, Bot Control, and rules that block odd request patterns. Add usage plans with API keys and per-merchant throttling, and reserved concurrency so one function cannot eat the whole account limit.
pay-card-testing.nudge: Put WAF between Users and API Gateway.

pay-fraud.title: Fraud scoring
pay-fraud.story: Every payment must now pass a fraud model that takes a few hundred ms: 20% of requests need scoring. Doing it inside the request keeps merchants waiting too long, and no payment may skip the check.
pay-fraud.concept: Lambda stores the payment as pending and sends a job to SQS with SSE-KMS; another Lambda pulls jobs and scores them. The queue KMS key policy must allow both functions, or the messages cannot be read.
pay-fraud.nudge: Add an encrypted SQS fed by Lambda, and a second Lambda reading from it.

pay-receipts.title: Receipts and reconciliation
pay-receipts.story: Besides fraud scoring, every payment must send the customer a receipt and post to the reconciliation system. The two jobs are independent: one being slow must not slow the other.
pay-receipts.concept: Lambda publishes to SNS, which fans out to two SQS queues, each with its own Lambda. Encrypt both queues; the SNS topic also supports SSE with KMS, and each queue access policy only lets that one topic send to it.
pay-receipts.nudge: Replace SQS with SNS → 2 SQS (encrypted), each with its own Lambda.

click-ingest.title: One stream, two readers
click-ingest.story: Every click on the marketplace must reach both the live dashboard and the fraud detection model, in order, and stay replayable when the model is retrained.
click-ingest.concept: Real-time, ordered, many apps reading one stream, replay → Kinesis Data Streams. SQS hands each message to one consumer and deletes it; SNS keeps nothing to replay. To just load into S3/Redshift with no code, use Data Firehose.
click-ingest.nudge: API Gateway → Kinesis → 2 Lambdas (dashboard, fraud) → DynamoDB.

click-eu.title: European customers
click-eu.story: The marketplace expands to Europe and 80% of users are now in the EU. Legal reminds you that under GDPR their click data must not leave the EU.
click-eu.concept: Data residency: pick an EU Region for every data store (stream, table, bucket). Use an SCP in AWS Organizations with the aws:RequestedRegion condition to block resources in other Regions. Trap: a global table copies the data out of the EU.
click-eu.nudge: Move API Gateway, Kinesis, both Lambdas and DynamoDB to eu-west-1.

click-encrypt.title: Encryption audit
click-encrypt.story: The GDPR auditor asks for every click to be encrypted at rest, both in the stream and in the table.
click-encrypt.concept: Kinesis Data Streams supports server-side encryption with KMS (SSE-KMS) per stream; DynamoDB is always encrypted and can use a customer managed key. Producers and consumers need kms:GenerateDataKey/Decrypt on that key.
click-encrypt.nudge: Turn on encryption for Kinesis and DynamoDB.

click-ransom.title: Ransomware
click-ransom.story: A developer's access key leaked. If the attacker deletes the table, the whole fraud history is gone.
click-ransom.concept: Turn on point-in-time recovery (PITR) or AWS Backup for DynamoDB to restore to any second in the last 35 days. Trap: a global table or replica is not a backup, since it copies the delete too. Use AWS Backup Vault Lock so the attacker cannot delete the backups.

click-peak.title: Black Friday
click-peak.story: Black Friday: clicks triple for a few hours. The stream will reject records (ProvisionedThroughputExceeded) without enough shards.
click-peak.concept: Each Kinesis shard takes 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s. Add shards before the peak (UpdateShardCount) or use on-demand mode. Lambda consumers read per shard, so more shards also means more parallel processing.
click-peak.nudge: Scale Kinesis up to medium (more shards).

fw-inspect.title: Inspect every packet
fw-inspect.story: The securities regulator requires all traffic into the platform to pass through the third-party firewall/IDS appliances the company licensed: 500 requests/s, account data encrypted, no server exposed to the internet.
fw-inspect.concept: Gateway Load Balancer sends traffic through a fleet of third-party security appliances (GENEVE, port 6081) before it reaches the app. WAF only filters layer 7 HTTP with rules; it does not replace IDS/IPS packet inspection.
fw-inspect.nudge: Users → GWLB → ALB → EC2 (2 instances, both a and b) → RDS (encryption on).

fw-partners.title: Partners need static IPs
fw-partners.story: Partner brokers only open their firewalls to a fixed list of IP addresses. The load balancer DNS name keeps changing IPs, so they cannot connect.
fw-partners.concept: Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs and brings traffic onto the AWS backbone. ALB and GWLB have no fixed IPs; for static IPs put Global Accelerator in front or use an NLB.
fw-partners.nudge: Add Global Accelerator between the users and the GWLB.

fw-fix.title: FIX orders over TCP
fw-fix.story: Institutional clients place orders with the FIX protocol over raw TCP, 30% of traffic. The ALB only speaks HTTP, so every FIX session is refused.
fw-fix.concept: NLB balances layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS) with ultra low latency. ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront and WAF are HTTP only. An NLB takes no WAF: protect it from DDoS with Shield Advanced.
fw-fix.nudge: Link the GWLB to a new NLB, and the NLB to a new EC2 group (2 instances, both a and b) for FIX.

fw-az.title: An AZ fails mid-session
fw-az.story: In the middle of the trading day, one us-east-1 AZ loses power. The platform cannot stop matching orders, not even for a few minutes.
fw-az.concept: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over in 1–2 minutes. EC2 groups spread over 2 AZs keep serving from the healthy one.
fw-az.nudge: Turn on Multi-AZ for RDS and check that every EC2 group runs in both a and b.

fw-ransom.title: Ransomware
fw-ransom.story: An employee's access key leaked. The attacker could wipe the orders and accounts database.
fw-ransom.concept: Multi-AZ and read replicas copy the delete too, so they are not backups. AWS Backup (with vault lock) or automated snapshots/PITR keep a separate copy to restore from.

wallet-ledger.title: A ledger in the EU
wallet-ledger.story: An e-wallet startup got its license in Ireland: 400 requests/s, 40% transactions written to a relational ledger. All data must stay in the EU, database passwords must rotate, and the old Lambda code once exhausted Aurora connections.
wallet-ledger.concept: Each Lambda environment opens its own connection, so under load a relational database runs out of connections. RDS Proxy pools them, fails over faster and reads the password from Secrets Manager, which rotates it. Aurora KMS encryption must be on when the cluster is created.
wallet-ledger.nudge: Everything in eu-west-1: API Gateway → Lambda → RDS Proxy → Aurora (encrypted); link RDS Proxy to Secrets Manager.

wallet-login.title: Customer sign-in
wallet-login.story: The mobile app is about to launch. Customers need to sign up, sign in with Apple or Google and turn on MFA before sending money.
wallet-login.concept: A Cognito user pool issues JWTs; API Gateway checks them with a Cognito authorizer. App customers use Cognito; employees use IAM Identity Center. Data must still stay in eu-west-1.
wallet-login.nudge: Link API Gateway to Cognito and keep every component in eu-west-1.

wallet-bots.title: Account-probing bots
wallet-bots.story: A botnet is trying sign-ins and transfer calls in bulk: strange traffic jumps 6× and drags Lambda and Aurora with it.
wallet-bots.concept: WAF with rate-based rules and managed rule groups blocks bots at API Gateway or CloudFront. Shield Standard covers layer 3/4 attacks for free; buy Shield Advanced for DRT support and cost protection.
wallet-bots.nudge: Put WAF between the users and API Gateway.

wallet-ransom.title: An attacker in the account
wallet-ransom.story: An IAM user was taken over and the attacker is trying to delete the ledger cluster. Losing the ledger means losing the license.
wallet-ransom.concept: Aurora has automated backups and PITR; AWS Backup adds central schedules, vault lock and cross-account copies. A read replica or Global Database will not help, since it replicates the delete. Turn on deletion protection for the cluster.

wallet-us.title: Customers in the US
wallet-us.story: The wallet expands to the US: 40% of users are now near us-east-1 and say the app is slow. The law still keeps data in the EU, so the database cannot be copied to the US.
wallet-us.concept: When data cannot move closer to users, bring users onto the AWS network early: CloudFront reaches the origin over the backbone and caches read responses. Trap: Aurora Global Database or a DynamoDB global table would break data residency.
wallet-us.nudge: Add CloudFront (cache API on) between WAF and API Gateway; keep the database in eu-west-1.

hr-signin.title: Who is signing in?
hr-signin.story: The company wants to drop its payroll spreadsheets for a web portal: 200 requests/s, 70% viewing profiles. The old prototype left the API open to anyone who knew the URL.
hr-signin.concept: A Cognito user pool handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA and federation with Google or the company SAML IdP. API Gateway uses a Cognito authorizer to check the JWT before calling Lambda, so the code never does auth itself. Use an identity pool only when the browser needs temporary AWS credentials.
hr-signin.nudge: Users → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB (encrypted); link API Gateway to Cognito.

hr-payslips.title: PDF payslips
hr-payslips.story: Every month staff download their payslip PDF: 800 requests/s, 60% file downloads. Lambda reads and returns each file itself, which is slow and billed per request. Payslips must never be exposed to the internet.
hr-payslips.concept: Keep static files in S3 and serve them through CloudFront with Origin Access Control and S3 Block Public Access on. Lambda only issues short-lived signed URLs. Common traps: a public bucket for convenience, or streaming large files through Lambda.
hr-payslips.nudge: Users → CloudFront; CloudFront → S3 for files and CloudFront → API Gateway for the API. Never link users straight to S3.

hr-ransom.title: A leaked access key
hr-ransom.story: A developer pushed an access key to a public GitHub repo. Security warns that an attacker could wipe the staff table and the payslip bucket at any moment.
hr-ransom.concept: Replication and global tables are not backups: they copy the delete too. Restore with AWS Backup (vault lock, cross-account copies), DynamoDB PITR and S3 versioning with Object Lock. Revoke the key and move to IAM roles.
hr-ransom.nudge: Turn on Backup on DynamoDB and S3.

hr-eu.title: The European branch
hr-eu.story: The company bought a firm in Ireland and 90% of staff are now in the EU. Legal reminds you that under GDPR, HR data must stay in the EU.
hr-eu.concept: Put the bucket, table and functions in eu-west-1 with no global copy in another Region. Across an organization, an SCP in AWS Organizations with an aws:RequestedRegion condition stops every account from creating resources outside allowed Regions.
hr-eu.nudge: Move S3, DynamoDB, API Gateway and Lambda to eu-west-1 and keep Backup on.

hr-bots.title: Credential stuffing
hr-bots.story: Passwords leaked from another site are being tried in bulk on the sign-in page: strange traffic jumps 6×, Lambda runs nonstop and the bill soars.
hr-bots.concept: AWS WAF with rate-based rules, Bot Control and the ATP (Account Takeover Prevention) rule group stops bots before they reach the API. Cognito advanced security adds adaptive MFA. A GWLB or security groups cannot filter the application layer.
hr-bots.nudge: Put WAF between the users and CloudFront.

crm-lift.title: Lift and shift
crm-lift.story: The data center closes at the end of the month. The old CRM (one web app and one MySQL database) must run on AWS now, with no time to change code. 400 requests/s, budget $125.
crm-lift.concept: Lift-and-shift (rehost): move servers as they are with AWS Application Migration Service and the database with DMS. Fastest and least risky; optimise costs in later steps.
crm-lift.nudge: ALB → EC2 (medium, 2 instances, AZ a and b) → RDS (medium).

crm-nights.title: The ops team quits
crm-nights.story: The only server admin just quit, and at night almost nobody uses the CRM while the EC2 fleet keeps billing. Management wants no servers and a bill under $100.
crm-nights.concept: Lambda bills per request, which suits load that rises and falls with the day. But each Lambda environment opens its own connection to RDS, so the database runs out of connections at peak. RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections, far cheaper than a bigger RDS.
crm-nights.nudge: Replace EC2 with Lambda behind the ALB and put RDS Proxy between Lambda and RDS (keep RDS medium).

crm-rotate.title: Passwords in code
crm-rotate.story: An audit found the database password sitting in an environment variable, unchanged for 3 years. From now on it must rotate automatically.
crm-rotate.concept: Secrets Manager stores the password, encrypts it with KMS and rotates it on a schedule. RDS Proxy reads it from Secrets Manager, so the app never sees it. Parameter Store has no built-in rotation.
crm-rotate.nudge: Add Secrets Manager and link RDS Proxy to it.

crm-reports.title: Quarter-end reports
crm-reports.story: At quarter end, sales keeps dashboards open all day: traffic rises to 850 requests/s, nearly all reads. RDS is overloaded and the budget allows only $18 more.
crm-reports.concept: When most traffic is repeated reads, a cache in front of the database (ElastiCache) is cheaper than a bigger RDS. Lambda checks the cache first and only asks the database on a miss (cache-aside).
crm-reports.nudge: Add ElastiCache and link Lambda to it; keep RDS medium.

crm-ransom.title: Ransomware
crm-ransom.story: An employee's access key leaked on GitHub. If an attacker deletes the database, the CRM must recover without losing customer data.
crm-ransom.concept: Separate backups (AWS Backup, automated snapshots, point-in-time restore) are the only way back from a deletion. Multi-AZ and read replicas copy the delete too, so they are not backups. AWS Backup Vault Lock stops attackers from deleting the backups.

partner-allowlist.title: IP allow-list
partner-allowlist.story: Partner banks only let their servers call a fixed list of IP addresses: 400 requests/s. Data must be encrypted and no server exposed to the internet.
partner-allowlist.concept: An NLB has one static IP (or Elastic IP) per AZ, so partners can allow-list it. An ALB DNS name resolves to IPs that change over time.
partner-allowlist.nudge: Users → NLB → EC2 (2 instances, both a and b) → RDS (encryption on).

partner-secrets.title: No hard-coded passwords
partner-secrets.story: Auditors found the database password in a config file on EC2, unchanged since launch. New policy: credentials rotate every 30 days.
partner-secrets.concept: Secrets Manager stores credentials encrypted with KMS and rotates them with a built-in Lambda for RDS. Parameter Store is cheaper but has no built-in rotation. The app reads the secret through the EC2 IAM role.

partner-files.title: Report files for partners
partner-files.story: Partners download daily reconciliation files: traffic grows to 800 requests/s, half of them downloads. Reading files from EBS overloads EC2. Security says servers must not reach the internet.
partner-files.concept: Move files to S3 to offload the servers. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3/DynamoDB is free and keeps traffic on the AWS network; a NAT gateway goes over the internet and charges per GB processed.
partner-files.nudge: EC2 → VPC Endpoint → S3 for static files.

partner-ransom.title: Ransomware wipes data
partner-ransom.story: An access key leaked on GitHub. The attacker could delete both the database and the reconciliation bucket.
partner-ransom.concept: Turn on S3 Versioning (plus Object Lock to block deletes) and backups/PITR for RDS with AWS Backup. Cross-Region replication is not a backup, since it replicates the delete too.
partner-ransom.nudge: Turn on Backup for both RDS and S3.

partner-az.title: An AZ goes down
partner-az.story: One us-east-1 AZ fails right when partners run their end-of-day reconciliation.
partner-az.concept: RDS Multi-AZ fails over to the standby in another AZ. Auto Scaling replaces the EC2 instances lost in the healthy AZ; the NLB only sends to healthy targets.
partner-az.nudge: Turn on Multi-AZ for RDS and Auto Scaling (max 4) for EC2.

rt-udp.title: Matches over UDP
rt-udp.story: A new shooter just launched: 85% of traffic is UDP packets carrying match state, the rest is player profile reads. Every millisecond of lag makes players quit.
rt-udp.concept: An ALB only speaks HTTP/HTTPS (layer 7). For non-HTTP TCP/UDP, ultra low latency or static IPs, use an NLB (layer 4). A GWLB only inserts security appliances; it does not serve games.
rt-udp.nudge: Users → NLB → EC2 (large, 2 instances, AZ a and b) → DynamoDB.

rt-global.title: European players
rt-global.story: The tournament opens to Europe: half the players are near eu-west-1 and complain about ping. The target is under 120 ms on average.
rt-global.concept: Global Accelerator gives 2 static anycast IPs and puts packets on the AWS backbone at the edge closest to players, for TCP and UDP alike. CloudFront only caches HTTP content, so it does nothing for UDP match traffic.
rt-global.nudge: Put Global Accelerator between Users and the NLB.

rt-events.title: Anti-cheat
rt-events.story: Every match now sends telemetry (10% of traffic). The anti-cheat team and the analytics team both need every event in order, and want to replay them when they retrain models.
rt-events.concept: Kinesis Data Streams keeps records in order per shard and lets several consumers read and replay them within the retention period. SQS deletes a message once one worker handles it, so two apps cannot both read it or replay it.

rt-tournament.title: The finals
rt-tournament.story: The finals are streamed live: players triple for one time slot. The budget cannot keep a fleet of big instances running all day.
rt-tournament.concept: Target tracking Auto Scaling adds instances as load climbs and removes them after the event. Pick an instance size where one covers normal play, then let the group grow at the peak; it costs less than keeping many big instances around.
rt-tournament.nudge: EC2 xlarge, minimum 1, Auto Scaling on, maximum 3.

rt-region.title: Region down mid-tournament
rt-region.story: us-east-1 fails in the middle of the tournament. Players must not drop out of matches, and match results must survive on both continents.
rt-region.concept: Run a copy of the game in each Region behind one Global Accelerator: health checks move players to the surviving Region within seconds. DynamoDB Global Tables take writes in both Regions, so losing one keeps the data.
rt-region.nudge: Global Accelerator → Route 53 → NLB + EC2 + Kinesis in each Region (eu-west-1 for the second); turn on Global for DynamoDB.

render-web.title: No ops team
render-web.story: A video render startup has two developers and nobody to patch operating systems or manage servers. The API already ships as a container.
render-web.concept: "Least operational overhead" + containers → ECS on Fargate: set CPU and memory per task, and AWS runs the servers and spreads tasks across AZs. The EC2 launch type is a bit cheaper but you manage the instances.

render-jobs.title: 30-minute renders
render-jobs.story: Customers start sending videos to render: 15% of requests are jobs that run 20–40 minutes. Doing them in the API makes users wait, and every job must finish.
render-jobs.concept: Jobs over 15 minutes break the Lambda timeout. Put them in SQS and let a separate Fargate service work through them (or AWS Batch). Set the visibility timeout longer than the job so the message is not handed out again halfway.
render-jobs.nudge: Add SQS linked from the web Fargate, and a worker Fargate (×2) reading from SQS. Don't use Lambda as the worker.

render-egress.title: No internet path
render-egress.story: Security finds that tasks in private subnets reach DynamoDB through a NAT gateway: data goes over the internet and the NAT bill grows with every GB.
render-egress.concept: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free, add a route to the route table and keep traffic on the AWS network. Other services (SQS, Secrets Manager…) use interface endpoints (PrivateLink), billed per hour. Classic trap: keeping the NAT gateway and buying more bandwidth.
render-egress.nudge: Put a VPC Endpoint between the web Fargate and DynamoDB: Fargate → VPC Endpoint → DynamoDB.

render-spot.title: Cheap renders
render-spot.story: Management wants render costs down. A render can be rerun if it is cut off, but the queue must be empty by the end of the day.
render-spot.concept: Fargate Spot is about 70% cheaper and can be reclaimed with a 2-minute notice: a fit for interruptible jobs when the work waits safely in SQS. Leave spare capacity to catch up on the backlog after an interruption.
render-spot.nudge: Switch the worker Fargate to Spot and use one large task so the queue drains after the interruption.

render-cycle.title: Quiet nights
render-cycle.story: Customers mostly work office hours: daytime traffic doubles, and at night it drops to 30%. Keeping enough tasks for the peak all night breaks the budget.
render-cycle.concept: ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking (CPU or requests per target) adds tasks by day and removes them at night. For a fixed daily pattern, add scheduled scaling to scale out before the peak. Watch it in CloudWatch.
render-cycle.nudge: Web Fargate: turn on Auto Scaling, minimum 1, maximum 4.

bill-api.title: Invoice API
bill-api.story: Business customers call the API to create and look up invoices: 900 requests/s, mostly reads. Budget $200.
bill-api.concept: Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible, keeps 6 copies across 3 AZs and handles more load than RDS of the same size. Spread EC2 over 2 AZs behind an ALB so one AZ is not a single point of failure.
bill-api.nudge: ALB → EC2 (medium, 3 instances, AZ a and b) → Aurora (medium).

bill-office.title: Office hours only
bill-office.story: Customers only work during office hours; at night traffic drops to 30% while 3 EC2 instances keep running. The budget drops to $168.
bill-office.concept: A fixed fleet sized for the peak pays for idle servers at night. Auto Scaling with a low minimum adds instances in the morning and removes them in the evening. For load with a known schedule, add scheduled scaling.
bill-office.nudge: Turn on Auto Scaling for EC2: minimum 1, maximum 4 medium instances.

bill-exports.title: PDF invoices
bill-exports.story: Half the requests now download PDF invoices, and servers reading files from their own disks are struggling. Files must live in S3, and servers in private subnets may not reach the internet. Budget $165.
bill-exports.concept: Move files to S3 to offload EC2. EC2 in a private subnet reaching S3 through a NAT gateway uses the internet path and pays data processing per GB; a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB is free and keeps traffic on the AWS network.
bill-exports.nudge: Add S3 and a VPC Endpoint: EC2 → VPC Endpoint → S3.

bill-reports.title: Month-end reports
bill-reports.story: On the last day of the month customers run reports nonstop: traffic climbs to 2,300 requests/s, almost all reads. Aurora is overloaded.
bill-reports.concept: A read replica takes read queries for less than a bigger Aurora. It copies asynchronously, so it can lag slightly: use it for reports and keep writes on the primary. Aurora's reader endpoint spreads reads across replicas.
bill-reports.nudge: Add a Read Replica (medium), link Aurora → Read Replica and EC2 → Read Replica. Set EC2 Auto Scaling to minimum 2, maximum 8.

bill-ransom.title: Ransomware
bill-ransom.story: An access key leaked. An attacker could delete both the database and the PDF invoice bucket. Accounting law requires keeping invoices for 10 years.
bill-ransom.concept: A read replica copies the delete too, so it is not a backup. Turn on Aurora backups (point-in-time restore) and S3 versioning with Object Lock so files cannot be deleted or overwritten. AWS Backup manages backups centrally.
bill-ransom.nudge: Turn on Backup for Aurora and S3.

udp-match.title: Matches over UDP
udp-match.story: The shooter runs its matches over UDP. The ALB only speaks HTTP, so every in-game packet gets dropped.
udp-match.concept: An ALB works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS, path and host routing). An NLB works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS): a static IP per AZ, ultra low latency, millions of connections. UDP, static IPs or ultra low latency in a question point to NLB.
udp-match.nudge: Swap the ALB for an NLB: Users → NLB → EC2 → DynamoDB.

packet-inspection.title: Inspect every packet
packet-inspection.story: Compliance wants all traffic to pass through a third-party firewall/IDS fleet before it reaches the servers. The WAF does not count.
packet-inspection.concept: A Gateway Load Balancer sends traffic through a fleet of third-party security appliances (GENEVE) and then on to the app. WAF only filters layer 7 HTTP and is not an IDS/IPS. Keywords: "third-party virtual appliance", "deep packet inspection".
packet-inspection.nudge: Swap the WAF for a GWLB: Users → GWLB → ALB → EC2 → RDS.

long-renders.title: Thirty-minute jobs
long-renders.story: Each video takes about 30 minutes to render. The Lambda worker is stopped at minute 15, so the queue never empties.
long-renders.concept: Lambda runs for 15 minutes at most. Longer jobs belong in containers on Fargate: no servers to manage, just CPU and memory per task. "Least operational overhead" with containers → Fargate; large batch fleets → AWS Batch.
long-renders.nudge: Replace the Lambda worker behind SQS with Fargate (medium).

replay-stream.title: Two teams, one stream
replay-stream.story: Analytics and fraud both need every click in order, and must replay old data when they fix a model. SQS hands each message to one consumer and deletes it.
replay-stream.concept: Kinesis Data Streams keeps records in order per shard for 1 to 365 days; many consumers read independently and can replay. SQS fits when each task needs one worker. Loading S3/Redshift with no code → Data Firehose.
replay-stream.nudge: API Gateway → Kinesis → two Lambdas (stats, fraud) → DynamoDB.

sign-in.title: Sign-in required
sign-in.story: The API is open to anyone. From next week, only registered customers may call it.
sign-in.concept: A Cognito user pool handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA and social sign-in; API Gateway checks the JWT with a Cognito authorizer. An identity pool trades the token for temporary AWS credentials. Employees use IAM Identity Center.

db-connections.title: Out of connections
db-connections.story: Every traffic jump makes hundreds of Lambdas open connections to RDS, and the database answers "too many connections". Its password is hard-coded too.
db-connections.concept: RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections, speeds up failover and reads its password from Secrets Manager. Secrets Manager rotates RDS passwords on its own; Parameter Store does not. DynamoDB uses IAM roles, so it needs no secret.
db-connections.nudge: Lambda → RDS Proxy → RDS, and link RDS Proxy to Secrets Manager.

private-path.title: Stay off the internet
private-path.story: EC2 sits in private subnets and reaches DynamoDB through a NAT gateway: out over the internet and billed per GB processed.
private-path.concept: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and added to route tables; traffic stays on the AWS network. Other services use interface endpoints (PrivateLink), billed per hour. Swapping NAT for a gateway endpoint is a classic cost question.
private-path.nudge: Put a VPC Endpoint between EC2 and DynamoDB.

ransomware.title: Ransomware
ransomware.story: An access key leaked, and the attacker is about to delete the database.
ransomware.concept: Replication is not backup: Multi-AZ, read replicas and global copies replicate the delete too. Use AWS Backup (with Vault Lock), PITR or S3 versioning with Object Lock to restore to a point before the attack.
ransomware.nudge: Select RDS and turn on Backup.

eu-only.title: Keep data in the EU
eu-only.story: Most customers are in Europe, and legal reminds you that under GDPR their data must not leave the EU.
eu-only.concept: Keep every data store in an EU Region with no global copy elsewhere. At the organization level, an SCP in AWS Organizations can deny resources in other Regions (aws:RequestedRegion).
eu-only.nudge: Move API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB to eu-west-1.
